title: JavaScript, the DOM and the event loop
subtitle: JavaScript runs one thing at a time — yet handles clicks, timers and network replies. The event loop is the trick.

sections.title: The language in brief
sections.body: Variables: let, const (block-scoped; prefer const). Types: number, string, boolean, null, undefined, object, array, function. Functions are values: const add = (a, b) => a + b. Use ===, not ==, to avoid coercion surprises (0 == '0' is true).

sections.title: The DOM and events
sections.body: The DOM is the page as a tree of objects. document.querySelector('#btn') finds a node; el.textContent = … changes it; el.addEventListener('click', fn) reacts. Events bubble up from the target to ancestors, so one listener on a list can handle all its items (event delegation).

choices.text: Travels from the target up through its ancestors.

sections.title: The event loop
sections.body: JavaScript has one call stack. Slow work (timers, network, I/O) is handed to the browser; when it finishes, a callback is queued. The event loop moves a queued callback onto the stack only when the stack is empty. Microtasks (promise callbacks) run before the next macrotask (timer, event).

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The callback waits until the stack is empty.

figures.caption: Figure 2.3.1 — timer and event loop
figures.note: A 0 ms timer still waits for the stack to empty.

sections.title: Promises and async/await
sections.body: A Promise represents a future value: pending → fulfilled or rejected. await pauses an async function (not the thread) until the promise settles: const res = await fetch(url); const data = await res.json();. Handle failure with try/catch; run independent requests together with Promise.all.

worked.why: Two independent requests take 300 ms and 200 ms.
Sequential: 500 ms. With Promise.all: the max of the two.

questions.prompt: Promise.all([a, b]) of 300 ms and 200 ms calls takes about…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: They run concurrently; total is the slowest.

problems.prompt: Three independent fetches take 100, 250 and 150 ms. Time with Promise.all vs one after another?

sections.title: Fetch in action
sections.body: A click handler calls fetch('/api/items'), awaits JSON and updates the DOM — no page reload. The browser’s same-origin policy blocks reading responses from other origins unless the server allows it via CORS headers.

questions.prompt: CORS is a rule enforced by…

choices.text: The browser, based on server headers.

sections.title: Frameworks and state
sections.body: Frameworks (React, Vue, Svelte) describe the UI as a function of state: change the state and the framework updates only the DOM parts that differ (virtual DOM or fine-grained reactivity). Keep state minimal, derive the rest, and lift shared state up to the nearest common parent.
